Title:
Fuel Treatment Technology
Introduction

This document covers the problems 
associated with use of heavy fuels which can be substantially reduced or 
eliminated by chemical modification of these fuels through incorporation of 
fireside additives. Fireside additives can improve power plant performance and 
extend equipment life.

Fireside additives are gaining wider 
recognization in combating problems related to boiler performance and 
reliability mainly corrosion, fouling, superheat control, acidic emissions and 
fly ash control.
Information
Boiler Fuel Problems

The problems-causing contaminates most often found 
in heavy fuels are listed in Table1. They compromise compounds of metals, 
especially vanadium, sodium, lead, potassium, and the non-metal, sulfur. When fuels containing these elements are burned, mixtures of oxides and sulfates 
are formed, collectively comprising fuel ash.
Table 1 Analysis Range For Heavy Oil Fuel

Fuel 
 Characteristics
Characteristics
Analysis
Ash
Analysis

Fireside problems can arise in three major areas of 
a boiler as shown in figure 1. In the furnace area and convection section (superheater 
and reheater), where temperature exceed 500ºC 
(~900ºF) deposits 
due to vanadium, sodium, lead, and potassium, can accumulate and reduce heat 
transfer. Corrosion of metal tubes and invasion of refractories can also occur 
if the deposits are in the molten or semi molten state. In the colder areas of 
the boiler (air preheater and stack) where temperatures may fall below the acid 
dew point

(below 150ºC /300ºF)
sulfuric acid formed from sulfur in the fuel 
can condense on metal surfaces and destroy them through acidic attack. Another 
problem area that arise in a heavy-fueled boiler operation is smoking and soot 
emission, due to incomplete combustion. Fuel additives are provides specialized 
oil-soluble additives to combat each of these problems. In addition, supplies 
additives to solve fuel handling problems-cold flow improves, pour point 
depressants and dispersants.
High Temperature Corrosion and Deposits

When a fuel containing vanadium and sodium are 
 burned in a boiler, ash components consisting of low-melting vanadium and 
 sodium oxides and sulfates are formed. Table 2 shows many of the possible ash 
 materials that can be formed in combustion of contaminated fuels. Although 
 vanadium alone can be a severe problem in causing deposits (V2O5 
 melts at 675ºC/1247ºF), 
 this temperature easily reached in the superheater and reheater sections of 
 boiler. At superheater temperatures, these ash components begin to soften and 
 impact and adhere to hot boiler surfaces, causing heavy tenacious deposits 
 which impede the free flow of gases in the boiler and reduce heat transfer. 
 This, in turn, causes a drop in steam temperatures and a loss of steam 
 production. If also forces the boiler operator to increase fuel consumption in 
 order to maintain design steam temperatures and pressures.

If the melting point of fuel ash is low 
 enough, semi-molten or molten deposits can attack the metal surfaces (superheater 
 and reheater tubes and hangers). This represents vanadic corrosion or high 
 temperature corrosion in a boiler.

Two methods may be effective 
 for controlling heavy ash deposits (slag) and high temperature corrosion.

Using of a fuel oil additives 
 capable of serving two functions.
 1- Increase the fusion point of the ash components to a point above the 
 prevailing temperatures in the superheater and reheater areas of the boiler. 
 2- Modify the ash that form friable form that won't result in hard deposits 
 and which can be easily removed by normal soot-blowing or (upon shutdown) by 
 water-washing (not high-pressure hydroplasting).

Choice of Inhibitor Metals
Magnesium

Magnesium is used to increase fusion point 
temperatures of boiler ash. Other alkaline earth-metal additives could be used, 
but most have disadvantages; e.g. Barium and Calcium form very hard-to-remove 
deposits. If Magnesium is incorporated in the fuel in a sufficiently available 
and active form, it will react in the flame with Vanadium oxides to form higher 
melting Magnesium vanadates, some of which are shown in Table 3. This vanadates 
melt at temperature well above those normally occuring in the convection 
sections of boilers.

Table 3 Increasing Melting Points of Ash 
Components By Additive Metals
(Lewis, D.C. and Goldberg, H.J., Combustion, p.31, December, 1978)
Aluminum

When the Sodium content [or the (Na+K)/V 
 ratio] of vanadic fuels becomes substantial, 
 control of deposits and corrosion by Magnesium additives may falter, due to 
 a Sodium fluxing effect (see Table 2). We have found that a specific 
 element, Aluminum, is needed for Sodium control. Additives containing 
 Alumina (Al2O3) 
 due to its chemical passivity, its major effect is a physical one: ash 
 friability may be improved (via dilution) when large amounts of (Al2O3) 
 are employed. For Aluminum to be effective in controlling the fluxing effect 
 of Sodium in combustion ash, it must be available for chemical 
 reaction. Specifically, to invoke the high melting point effect of
 Aluminum on the Sodium content of fuels, 
 a highly reactive, oil-soluble or organometallic form of
 Aluminum is required such as unique oil-soluble 
 Aluminum compound (20% Aluminum) for use in fuel additives. Two aspects of 
 Aluminum's effect on Sodium are recognized.

React with some of the Magnesium to form 
 a crystalline material known as spinel (MgAl2O4) which help to retain the combustion 
 ash in the form of fine particles and in friable condition and this 
 chemical effect eliminates the extremely sticky and low-melting deposits 
 from mixtures of Sodium and Vanadium oxides.

sections.text:
Failure of Aluminum oxide to provide a 
 larger melting point increase (as would be expected from Table 3) is 
 understood to be due not to the limitations of Aluminum itself as a 
 slag modifier but to the unreactivity of granular (Al2O3).
Silicon

Silicon is of special value for physical modification of boiler combustion 
 ash-to keep the ash dry and friable. Oil soluble (organometallic) silicon 
 components of additives, when burned with the fuel, form superfine particles 
 of silicon dioxide which act to "coat" and dilute the particles. This effect 
 of silicon at temperatures which include both the boiler and gas turbine 
 operating regimes.

SO3 Generation and Cold-End 
Corrosion

When sulfur containing fuels are burned in a boiler, the sulfur emerges 
 largely as SO2; however, a very small amount of sulfur trioxide is also formed 
 in the flame reaction. If sulfur dioxide in the exhaust contact with Fe2O3 
 or V2O5 slag surfaces at temperatures of 500-6500C 
 (900-12000F), and extra oxygen is present in the flue gases to react 
 with it, SO3 will be formed in large quantities. This catalytic 
 reaction is shown as follows:

SO2 + O2 (Fe2O3, 
 V2O5) → SO3

At 
 temperatures below the acid dew point (generally less than 3000F, 
 the sulfur trioxide condenses out with water vapor to form highly corrosive H2SO4. 
 Condensation of this acid on metal parts as in an air preheater or in a 
 cold stack, will result in eventual failure of the corroded components from 
 what is called cold-end corrosion. Reduction of sulfur trioxide is an 
 important objective for boiler operator. There are three methods to solve that 
 problem.

items:
Reduce 
 excess air (and O2) to a point where SO2 to SO3 
 reaction can't occur.

Endeavour to neutralize the acid as it condenses in the cold sections of the 
 boiler.

Prevent 
 the acid from forming by eliminating the catalytic reaction in the high 
 temperature regions of the boiler.

sections.text: Suppress SO3

The most 
 practical method of suppressing SO3 generation in boiler operation 
 is to provide a continuing supply of superfine MgO having high specific 
 surface area and reactivity to coat catalytic surfaces of iron oxide and
 V2O5. 
 The most effective form of MgO is that generated by the combustion of 
 fuel containing an oil soluble Magnesium additive. At relatively low 
 concentrations in relation to sulfur content of fuels, oil soluble Magnesium 
 additives generating a nascent, superfine form of MgO, provide a degree 
 of effectiveness in suppressing the SO2-SO3 conversion 
 reaction.

These 
 applications involves fuels containing 5-25 ppm vanadium and 0.3-1.0% sulfur, 
 satisfactory control (down to a few ppm SO3) is achieved by use of 
 3-5 gallons per thousand barrels, representing a modest cost of price such 
 fuels (light blended residual oils). We employ severn science SO3 
 monitors to provide a continuous numerical record of SO3 control 
 in fuel tests and applications.

When 
 heavier boiler fuels are involved, ranging higher in either sulfur or vanadium 
 content, we anticipate successful control at higher dosages. When both sulfur 
 and vanadium contents are high, our experience suggests that SO3 
 control by even the best fuel treatment that may not be effective, so that 
 applications involving this class of fuel must be undertaken with due caution
Smoking and Soot Emissions

Another 
 problem in a boiler is that of smoking and inefficient combustion. This will 
 always occur when the excess oxygen level is insufficient to combust the fuel 
 completely, but it may also happen when a mechanical problem exists in the 
 boiler, such as worn or improperly adjusted oil guns in the burners. If the 
 soot and smoke generated by these problems is excessive, the fuel isn't being 
 efficiently burned and the overall efficiency of the boiler suffers. Air 
 pollution regulations may also be broken if the smoke is sufficient to exceed 
 the local air quality specifications.

In 
 correcting smoking problem, any needed mechanical adjustments should obviously 
 be made first such as proper adjustment, cleaning of burner nozzles, etc. If 
 smoking still occurs at reasonable excess air levels, an additive may be 
 needed. here, an oil-soluble form of Mn or other metal is used to promote 
 oxidation of the fuel. Through catalytic action of the Mn in the flame, the 
 carbonaceous components of the fuel are more completely burned and soot and 
 smoke are reduced. This obviously increases the efficiency of the boiler 
 because more of the fuel's heat content goes toward producing steam, not 
 smoke.
Smoke Control

Using 
 [25% Mn (conc.), or its diluted version, and 10% Mn (dil.)] to provide a 
 manganese level of about 25 to 50 ppm, may result in a dramatic lossening of 
 visible smoke. This may be sufficient to allow substantial reductions in 
 excess air to be made. In principle, major reductions in excess oxygen can 
 result in substantial improvements in overall boiler efficiency (in some 
 cases, as high as 5%).

Barium, 
 while it may be less effective as a soot scavenger, seems also to extra prior, 
 in flame action to prevent soot particle formation. Because of this difference 
 in their mechanism, barium may be more efficient than Mn combustion improves 
 in specific applications. Thus, use of a composition [25% Ba (conc.), or its 
 diluted form and 10% Ba (dil.)] to provide a Barium level of 25-100 ppm 
 may be effective if insufficient manganese response is observed.

Thus, 
 effective additive requirements for smoke suppression in boiler can't be 
 predicted simply from fuel composition and designation of equipment and 
 operating parameters. In applying smoke suppression additives, there is 
 substantial need for a convenient field instrument like the Von Brand Meter 
 for monitoring gas turbine, boiler, and diesel smoke suppression.
Recalculation of ppm-Results to mg/m3

Basics: 
 Avogardro's Number, Ideal Gas Law

ppm = parts 
 per million (by mass or by volume: mg/kg or ml/m3
 not: mg/l)

A similar 
 unit is % = parts per hundred 
 1% = 10.000 ppm

The 
 volume share is relevant when talking about gases !

6.023* 1023 
 atoms or molecules = 1 mole 
 (Avogardro's Number)

1 mole of 
 each gas 
 = 22.41 liters (Ideal Gas Law)

The mass of 
 1 mole 
 = Molecular weight in grams

e.g. 
 Carbon monoxide: C 
 O

Atomic 
 weights: 
 12+16 = 28 Molecular weight

Therefore: 1 mole of CO has a weight of 28 
 g and a volume of 22.41 l.
Recalculation procedure:

mg/m3 
 = ppm * molecular mass / 22.41

e.g. CO: mg/m3 
 = ppm * 28 / 22.41
